leadRef: Anthropic slips below its $83 IPO price as Nvidia gives back Monday's rally
description: Anthropic falls below its IPO price as the AI rally fades; a CIA intelligence system is breached; AI-assisted attackers hit Check Point firewall servers at 22 firms; OpenAI's GPT-6 designs proteins; Sanofi buys Insmed for $41bn; Huawei is convicted.

thirtySecond.p: An unclassified CIA and ODNI intelligence-analysis system was hacked, the latest in a run of US government breaches.
Attackers likely using AI agents got into Check Point management servers at 22 firms, including banks' peers in finance.
OpenAI says its general model designed proteins that bound all five lab targets, though specialist tools still filtered them.

footerNote: Wednesday's deep beat, security: a breached CIA intelligence system, AI-assisted intrusions into Check Point firewall managers and a financial firm's website, two infrastructure vendors leaking customers' cloud keys, Microsoft's 'Code Red' after its worst email outage, and a correction on Medicare drug-price timing.

stories.title: Anthropic shares close at $81.90 on 24 Nov, 6.5% down on the day and below their $83 IPO price four sessions after the record $81bn listing, as the Huang rally fades: Nvidia falls 5.9% to $155.38 after Monday's 31.5% jump, the Nasdaq loses 1.5% to 23,733.54 and the S&P 500 0.5% to 7,201.09, while the Dow gains 0.85% to 50,018.70; Fed futures price a 98% chance of a December hike before Wednesday's PCE inflation data
stories.h: Anthropic slips below its $83 IPO price as Nvidia gives back Monday's rally
stories.sub: Four sessions after the biggest listing on record, the Claude maker trades under its offer price; Nvidia drops 5.9% and the Nasdaq 1.5% while the Dow climbs back above 50,000.
stories.ticker: ANT closes $81.90 (-6.5%), below $83 IPO price; NVDA -5.9% to $155.38; Nasdaq -1.5%
stories.body:
Anthropic closed at $81.90 on Tuesday, down 6.5% and below the $83 price of its 19 Nov IPO, which raised about $81bn. The stock opened at $111.50 on its first day and has fallen in every session since. Nvidia gave back 5.9% to $155.38 after Monday's 31.5% surge on Jensen Huang's return. The Nasdaq fell 1.5% to 23,733.54 and the S&P 500 0.5%, while the Dow rose 0.85% to 50,018.70 as money rotated into older industries. Reuters quotes Cetera's Gene Goldman: one headline "doesn't really resolve investor questions about the AI trade". Fed funds futures price a 98% chance of a December rate rise and 66% for another in January; US PCE inflation data is due on Wednesday. Early on Wednesday, Tokyo's Nikkei fell more than 2%, led by chip stocks (WSJ).

So what: an AI IPO priced for a boom is already under water while rate rises are coming; banks with exposure to AI-linked lending, data-centre credit or margin books on these names should expect more volatility, not less, into the 9 Dec Fed decision.
stories.chip: Closing prices checked on Yahoo Finance chart data (opened); market narrative from Reuters via Mint (opened)
src: Reuters via Mint: US stocks slide as Nvidia rally fizzles out, dollar falls
WSJ: Nikkei falls 2.8%, dragged by chip-related stocks
stories.brief:
Anthropic listed on 19 Nov in the largest IPO on record, pricing at $83 a share. It opened at $111.50 and closed its first day at $97.17, then slid to $88.91, $87.64 and, on Tuesday, $81.90. That is the first close below the offer price.

The fall came as the market cooled after Monday, when Nvidia jumped 31.5% on Jensen Huang's reinstatement. On Tuesday Nvidia lost 5.9%, the Nasdaq 1.5% and the S&P 500 0.5%; the Dow rose 0.85% to just above 50,000. The 10-year Treasury yield was little changed at about 4.93%, Brent crude rose 2.3% to $91.40 on attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz, and gold fell 2.7%.

Investors are now waiting for Wednesday's PCE inflation figures, the last major data before the Fed's 8-9 Dec meeting, where a rate rise is almost fully priced.
facts: US PCE inflation, 25 Nov; Fed decision 9 Dec
stories.impactWho: Investors in AI stocks and the IPO pipeline (OpenAI, Nscale, Databricks), banks lending against AI collateral or underwriting AI deals, and anyone pricing December's rate rise.
stories.short: Anthropic closed at $81.90 on Tuesday, below its $83 IPO price, four sessions after the record listing. Nvidia gave back 5.9% after Monday's 31.5% jump and the Nasdaq fell 1.5%, while the Dow rose above 50,000. Markets price a 98% chance of a Fed rate rise in December.

stories.title: An unclassified open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system used by the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence was breached, the NYT reported on 24 Nov and AP and CyberScoop confirmed; a source says no classified networks were involved and the issue is resolved; it follows an apparent hack of an FBI criminal-justice database and an NSA classified network outage this month
stories.h: Hackers breach a CIA and ODNI open-source intelligence system
stories.ticker: Unclassified CIA/ODNI open-source intelligence system breached; no classified data, source says
stories.body:
An unclassified system that the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence use to analyse open-source intelligence (news, commercial satellite images, data-broker feeds) was breached, The New York Times reported on 24 Nov; AP and CyberScoop confirmed it through unnamed sources. A source told CyberScoop the hack "did not involve our classified networks"; AP's source says the issue has been resolved. It is not known what was taken or who did it; the CIA declined to comment. It follows an apparent hack of an FBI national criminal-justice database and a temporary outage of an NSA classified network this month. Huntress's Ben Bernstein notes that seeing what analysts search for reveals US intelligence priorities without touching a classified file.

So what: the US intelligence community's outward-facing tools are being hit in the same month as bank and cloud outages; banks that share threat data with government channels should assume those feeds can be watched.
stories.chip: Checked on CyberScoop and AP via SecurityWeek (both opened); NYT original not opened; no official statement
src: CyberScoop: Unclassified intel system hit by hackers, affecting CIA, ODNI
AP via SecurityWeek: An unclassified CIA system was breached in a cyberattack
stories.short: A CIA and ODNI system for analysing open-source intelligence was breached, the NYT reported and AP and CyberScoop confirmed. Sources say no classified networks were involved and the issue is resolved; what was taken and by whom is unknown. It follows an FBI database hack and an NSA network outage this month.

stories.title: GreyNoise reports (23 Nov) an intrusion campaign, tracked as GT13, against Check Point Security Management Servers at at least 22 organisations in 17 countries, including financial services, energy and government, between 17 Oct and 2 Nov; the actor used 99 IP addresses, a relay server holding data stolen from 24 management servers, and exploits including CVE-2026-16232 (SmartConsole authentication bypass), NetScaler, Ivanti and NetLogon flaws; GreyNoise believes LLMs and agents automated much of the work and expects the campaign is ongoing
stories.h: Attackers using AI tools broke into Check Point firewall management servers at 22 firms
stories.ticker: GreyNoise: GT13 campaign hit Check Point management servers at 22 orgs incl. finance; likely ongoing
stories.body:
Threat-intelligence firm GreyNoise says an unattributed actor it calls GT13 broke into Check Point Security Management Servers, which control firewall policy, at at least 22 organisations in 17 countries (UK, Ireland, France, Germany, India, South Korea, Hong Kong, Australia, the US and others) between 17 Oct and 2 Nov. Victims include financial services, energy, government and transport. The actor used 99 IP addresses and a compromised relay server that held data stolen from 24 management servers, and tried exploits including CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass, patched in July), Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti and Windows NetLogon flaws. GreyNoise says it saw hands-on-keyboard activity but believes the actor used LLMs and agents for scanning, exploitation and tool-building, and that the campaign is ongoing. It is notifying victims through CERTs.

So what: whoever owns a firewall's management server owns the firewall; banks running Check Point should confirm the July hotfix is on every management, log and SmartEvent server and hunt for the indicators GreyNoise published.
stories.chip: Checked on GreyNoise's own write-up (opened); Check Point has not commented in what we found
src: GreyNoise: An active intrusion campaign against Check Point Security Management Servers
Rapid7: CVE-2026-16232 Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass exploited
stories.short: GreyNoise says an actor it calls GT13 broke into Check Point firewall management servers at 22 organisations in 17 countries, including financial firms, between mid-October and early November, using a July authentication-bypass flaw among others. It believes AI agents automated much of the work and that the campaign continues.

stories.title: OpenAI says (24 Nov) its GPT-6 models can design new protein structures and sequences using only reasoning and general-purpose code, without specialised biology models; in lab tests with partner Onava, at least one protein from GPT-6.2's designs bound each of five targets and redesigned antibodies kept binding, though specialised models still supplied sequences, filtered and selected candidates
stories.h: OpenAI says GPT-6 can design working proteins without specialised biology models
stories.ticker: OpenAI: GPT-6.2 protein designs bound all five lab targets; specialised models still used to filter
stories.body:
OpenAI published a preprint, "GPT-6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology", saying its GPT-6 family can design new protein shapes and amino-acid sequences by reasoning and writing code, without calling specialised tools such as RFdiffusion or ProteinMPNN. An internal research model matched or beat specialised models on many design tasks. In lab tests with partner Onava, at least one small protein based on GPT-6.2's 3D designs showed binding for each of five targets, and many redesigned minibinders and antibodies kept binding. OpenAI is candid about limits: its hit rates were below the original RFdiffusion study, and specialised models (Boltz-2, ESMFold2) supplied sequences and filtered candidates, so the work "does not yet establish" a fully general-model pipeline.

So what: general models are starting to replace the specialist tools in drug discovery; biotech lenders and pharma investors should watch whether design costs and timelines actually fall.
stories.chip: Checked on OpenAI's own post (opened), including its limitations section; preprint not reviewed
src: OpenAI: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
stories.short: OpenAI says its GPT-6 models can design new proteins by reasoning and writing code, without specialised biology models. In lab tests, GPT-6.2 designs bound all five targets tried. OpenAI notes its hit rates trail specialist tools and that specialised models still filtered and selected the candidates.

stat.label: lab targets bound by GPT-6.2 designs

stories.title: Sanofi agrees (24 Nov) to buy Insmed for $175 a share, $41.0bn in cash, the largest biopharma deal in years, gaining Brinsupri (brensocatib, for bronchiectasis) and Arikayce plus the phase 3 inhaled TPIP programme, to offset the coming loss of Dupixent revenue; Sanofi expects it to add to earnings per share by the end of 2028
stories.h: Sanofi buys Insmed for $41bn to replace Dupixent's fading growth
stories.ticker: Sanofi to buy Insmed for $41bn ($175/share cash); gains Brinsupri and Arikayce
stories.body:
Sanofi will pay $175 a share, $41.0bn (EUR 37.6bn) in cash and debt-financed, for US biotech Insmed, the largest biopharma acquisition in years. It gets two approved lung medicines, Brinsupri (brensocatib, the first drug for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis) and Arikayce, plus a phase 3 inhaled therapy, TPIP. Sanofi, led by Belen Garijo, faces losing exclusivity on its blockbuster Dupixent; it expects the deal to add to earnings per share by the end of 2028 and to keep a strong credit rating. Insmed traded near $120 before Bloomberg reported talks on 19 Nov and closed at $170.15 on Tuesday.

So what: a $41bn cash deal means a large debt raise for Sanofi; for banks it is a big underwriting and lending mandate, and a sign that big pharma will pay up for approved drugs over pipelines.
stories.chip: Checked on Sanofi's press release and STAT (both opened); Insmed price from market data
src: Sanofi: Sanofi to acquire Insmed in strategic step that strengthens long-term future
STAT: Sanofi to buy Insmed for $41B, picking up two lung disease medicines
Endpoints: Sanofi to buy Insmed in industry's largest acquisition in years
stories.short: Sanofi will buy Insmed for $175 a share, $41bn in cash, the biggest biopharma deal in years. It gains two approved lung drugs, Brinsupri and Arikayce, and a phase 3 programme as its blockbuster Dupixent nears the end of exclusivity. Sanofi expects the deal to add to earnings by end-2028.

stories.title: A Brooklyn federal jury finds Huawei guilty (24 Nov) on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud over its Iran business and conspiracy to violate US sanctions, but acquits it of racketeering conspiracy; sentencing is set for September 2027 and Huawei is expected to appeal
stories.h: US jury convicts Huawei of trade-secret theft and bank fraud, clears it of racketeering
stories.ticker: Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts incl. trade secrets, bank fraud; acquitted of racketeering
stories.body:
After a two-month trial in Brooklyn, a jury found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets from rivals, bank fraud (lying to banks about its business in Iran) and conspiracy to violate US sanctions. It was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy, which required finding it acted as a criminal enterprise. Huawei says the acquittal "vindicates" its position. Charges were first brought in 2019 after the arrest of executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada. Sentencing is planned for September 2027; Huawei's lawyer expects an appeal.

So what: a bank-fraud conviction for misleading lenders about Iran dealings is a reminder that sanctions screening of large corporate clients is a criminal matter, not only a compliance one.
stories.chip: Checked on BBC (opened); CNA/Reuters and The Verge report the same verdict; DOJ statement not opened
src: BBC: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
CNA: China's Huawei convicted in sprawling US criminal trial over Iran business
The Verge: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
stories.short: A New York jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud over its Iran business and sanctions violations, but acquitted it of racketeering. Sentencing is set for September 2027, and Huawei is expected to appeal.

stories.title: Security startup Jesta reports (24 Nov, via The Register) that an attacker in Bucharest pointed the free open-source coding agent OpenCode, the Mac's built-in curl and Chrome at a major financial-services firm on 16 Nov and found an access key (a decoy) and ran an almost complete attack in under six minutes at no cost; the model used is unknown
stories.h: Free coding agent found a financial firm's access key in under six minutes
stories.ticker: Jesta: attacker used free OpenCode agent to find a (decoy) key at a financial firm in under 6 minutes
stories.body:
Tel Aviv security startup Jesta told The Register that on 16 Nov someone in Bucharest pointed OpenCode, a free open-source coding agent that works with 200+ model providers, at a major financial-services customer's website. Using only the agent, the Mac's built-in curl and Chrome, it tried several ways in and found an access key (a planted decoy) in under six minutes, at no cost to the operator. Jesta identified the agent from its web-fetch tool's signature; it does not know which model was used. "Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking," its CTO said, but nothing stops it being pointed at someone else's site.

So what: attacks no longer need special malware or pentest kits; banks should assume any exposed secret in web pages, JavaScript or repos will be found within minutes, and should seed decoy keys to detect it.
stories.chip: One outlet (The Register's exclusive, opened); Jesta's report not opened; the bank is unnamed
src: The Register: An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes
stories.short: Security firm Jesta says an attacker used OpenCode, a free open-source coding agent, plus curl and Chrome to probe a major financial firm and find an access key, a planted decoy, in under six minutes at no cost. The bank is unnamed and the model used is unknown; one outlet reports it.

stories.title: Two infrastructure vendors disclose breaches that exposed customer cloud secrets: Radware says (root-cause report via BleepingComputer, 24 Nov) an internal Cloud WAF management API reachable from the internet without authentication was accessed on 19 Nov, exposing customer contacts and, for some, log-export credentials for AWS S3, Azure Blob or SFTP; Rackspace is shutting its Rackspace Spot Kubernetes platform on 8 Dec after attackers used stolen credentials on 17 Nov to read customer cluster secrets
stories.h: Radware and Rackspace breaches expose customers' cloud keys and Kubernetes secrets
stories.ticker: Radware API breach exposed customers' S3/Azure log keys; Rackspace shuts Spot after cluster secrets read
stories.body:
Radware, which protects 12,500 enterprises and carriers, says an unauthorised party on 19 Nov accessed an internal Cloud WAF management API that was reachable from the internet without authentication. Exposed: customer contact details and, for some, the credentials used to export logs to their own AWS S3, Azure Blob or SFTP storage. It detected the breach ten hours later and tells AppSec customers to rotate those keys; some have seen AWS alerts from an unfamiliar IP. Separately, Rackspace is shutting down Rackspace Spot on 8 Dec after attackers used stolen credentials on 17 Nov to create pods in customer Kubernetes clusters and read cluster secrets.

So what: the security vendors in a bank's stack hold keys to its storage; ask every WAF, DDoS and cloud provider which of your credentials they keep, and rotate Radware log-export keys now if you use Cloud WAF.
stories.chip: Both from BleepingComputer (opened), quoting Radware's root-cause report and Rackspace's customer notice; neither company's own page opened
src: BleepingComputer: Radware discloses breach exposing customer cloud access keys
BleepingComputer: Rackspace shuts down Spot cloud platform after security breach
stories.short: Radware says an internal Cloud WAF API left open without authentication was accessed on 19 Nov, exposing customer contacts and some customers' S3, Azure and SFTP log-export keys. Rackspace is shutting its Spot Kubernetes platform on 8 Dec after attackers read customer cluster secrets.

stories.title: Microsoft declares an internal 'Code Red' after the near 24-hour Exchange Online and Microsoft 365 outage of 12-13 Nov, the most customer-affecting incident in Exchange Online's history, internal memos reported by Reuters show; it sets five workstreams (load shedding, geographic partitioning, faster recovery), a goal of resolving worldwide incidents within an hour with AI agents helping diagnosis, and notes one urgent fix took five to six days to reach all servers
stories.h: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after its worst-ever Exchange Online outage
stories.ticker: Microsoft 'Code Red' after 12-13 Nov M365 outage; targets one-hour fixes; urgent patch took 5-6 days
stories.body:
Internal memos reported by Reuters show Microsoft has declared a "Code Red", its highest internal priority, after the nearly 24-hour outage of Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams and Copilot on 12-13 Nov that hit governments, trading firms and airlines. Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson called it the most customer-affecting incident in Exchange Online's history and admitted past work "had not been enough". Another memo describes a "fog of war": responders exchanged over 11,000 messages in 11 Teams chats. The plan covers load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery, with a goal of fixing worldwide incidents within an hour; one urgent production fix took five to six days to reach every server.

So what: banks running email, trading chat and Copilot on one provider should test how they work through a full-day outage; Microsoft itself says it cannot yet push an urgent fix worldwide in an hour.
stories.chip: Checked on SiliconANGLE (opened), which reviewed the Reuters report; memos not seen directly
src: SiliconANGLE: Microsoft declares internal Code Red after nearly 24-hour Microsoft 365 outage
TNW: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after its worst email outage, Reuters reports
stories.short: Microsoft has declared an internal 'Code Red' after the nearly 24-hour Exchange Online and Microsoft 365 outage of 12-13 Nov, memos reported by Reuters show. It aims to fix worldwide incidents within an hour using AI agents; one urgent fix took five to six days to reach every server.

stories.title: South Korea's Financial Services Commission unveils a draft bill (24 Nov) that would initially let only bank-majority-owned groups issue won stablecoins (a fintech can be the largest single shareholder), require FSC authorisation, at least 5bn won of capital, 100% reserves and redemption at face value, cap shareholders' stakes in crypto exchanges at 20% (34% with approval) and lift the 2017 ban on domestic coin offerings
stories.h: South Korea's draft law hands won stablecoins to bank-led groups
stories.ticker: Korea FSC draft: bank-majority won stablecoins, 100% reserves, 20% cap on exchange stakes, ICOs back
stories.body:
South Korea's Financial Services Commission published a draft bill on Tuesday under which won-denominated stablecoins could at first be issued only by groups in which banks collectively own more than half, though a fintech or tech firm could be the largest single shareholder. Issuers would need FSC authorisation, at least 5bn won (about $3.7m) of capital, 100% reserves and redemption at face value without delay. Crypto exchanges would need dealing, brokerage and custody licences, and any shareholder would be capped at 20% (34% with approval). The bill would also lift the 2017 ban on domestic coin offerings. It settles a long fight: the central bank wanted banks in control; the FSC had favoured non-banks too. A Korean report says the won-stablecoin rollout may slip to 2028.

So what: another major economy is putting stablecoins inside the banking system rather than beside it; Korean banks become the gatekeepers, and foreign issuers face a bank-partnered route.
stories.chip: Checked on Cointelegraph (opened), which links the FSC announcement; FSC text not opened; 2028 timing from a Chosun headline only
src: Cointelegraph: South Korea proposes bank-led stablecoins, 20% cap on crypto exchange stakes
stories.short: South Korea's FSC has drafted a law under which bank-majority groups would issue won stablecoins, with 100% reserves, face-value redemption and at least 5bn won of capital. Shareholders in crypto exchanges would be capped at 20%, and the 2017 ban on domestic coin offerings would end.

stories.title: Dell raises its fiscal 2027 forecasts for the third time (24 Nov) after a record quarter: revenue now $202bn (from $192bn; analysts $194.5bn), AI-optimised server revenue $78bn (from $74bn) and adjusted EPS $29.68 (from $25.50), and adds a $25bn buyback; shares rise about 5% after hours; HP's quarterly revenue of $16bn also beats forecasts
stories.h: Dell lifts its AI server forecast to $78bn and adds a $25bn buyback
stories.ticker: Dell FY27 revenue guide $202bn; AI servers $78bn; $25bn buyback; shares +5% late
stories.body:
Dell raised its annual forecasts for the third time this year after a record quarter. It now expects fiscal 2027 revenue of $202bn (from $192bn; analysts expected $194.5bn), AI-optimised server revenue of $78bn (from $74bn) and adjusted EPS of $29.68 (from $25.50). The board approved another $25bn share buyback and shares rose about 5% after hours, recovering part of a 12% fall in Tuesday's session. Its PC business grew more slowly. Rival HP reported quarterly revenue of $16bn, above the $15.4bn expected.

So what: enterprise AI hardware spending is still rising even as AI stocks wobble; for banks, the data-centre capex cycle that backs much AI credit has not turned yet.
stories.chip: Checked on Reuters via CNA (opened) and Yahoo price data; Dell's release not opened
src: Reuters via CNA: Dell lifts annual forecasts after record quarter on surging AI server demand
The Defiant: Dell lifts outlook as AI server sales hit $22 billion
stories.short: Dell raised its forecasts for the third time this year: fiscal 2027 revenue of $202bn and AI server revenue of $78bn, up from $74bn. It added a $25bn buyback, and shares rose about 5% after hours. HP also beat revenue forecasts.

stories.title: PrismML releases Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B (24 Nov), a ternary-weight version of Qwen3.8 27B that fits in 5.9GB and scores 75.6 on SWE-bench Verified (base model 80.6; previous Bonsai 60.8) and 90.5 on AppWorld (base 93.2), running at 291 tokens/s on one H100 and 204 on an RTX 4090; it reaches 302 points on Hacker News
stories.h: A 27B ternary model in 5.9GB nearly matches its full-size base on coding agents
stories.ticker: PrismML Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B: 5.9GB, SWE-bench Verified 75.6 vs base 80.6
stories.body:
PrismML released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, which stores each weight as one of three values and keeps Qwen3.8 27B's abilities in a 5.9GB file. On its own benchmarks it scores 75.6 on SWE-bench Verified (full-precision base 80.6; its previous version 60.8), 90.5 on AppWorld (base 93.2) and 60.1 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (base 70.8). It runs at 291 tokens/s on one Nvidia H100 and 204 on a consumer RTX 4090. The update targets long chains of tool calls and fixes over-thinking loops in version 2. GGUF weights are on Hugging Face; the launch drew 302 points on Hacker News.

So what: a near-frontier coding agent that fits on a laptop GPU makes private, on-premises agents realistic for code and documents that cannot leave a bank; the scores are the company's own.
stories.chip: Checked on PrismML's own post (opened); benchmarks are the company's; Hugging Face listing seen in the collector
stories.short: PrismML's Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B stores weights as one of three values and fits in 5.9GB, yet scores 75.6 on SWE-bench Verified against 80.6 for its full-size Qwen base. It runs at 204 tokens a second on a consumer RTX 4090. The benchmarks are the company's own.

stories.title: Utah moves to drop criminal charges against Kalshi and its co-founders (24 Nov), a day after Kalshi halted trading in the state for its 177,000 users after losing court bids to block Utah's gambling-law enforcement; the CFTC separately replaces 17 prediction-market waivers with one permanent reporting rule
stories.h: Utah drops criminal charges after Kalshi leaves the state
stories.ticker: Utah moves to drop criminal case vs Kalshi after it halts trading for 177k Utah users
stories.body:
Kalshi paused operations in Utah on 23 Nov after losing court fights, including a federal appeals bid, to stop the state enforcing its gambling laws; a CFTC emergency motion arguing federal jurisdiction has not been granted. "This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi," its spokesperson said. A day later Utah's attorney general moved to drop criminal charges against the company and its co-founders. A New York judge had declined on 23 Nov to block Kalshi there for now. The CFTC also adopted a single permanent reporting rule for prediction markets in place of 17 separate waivers.

So what: state gambling law is winning the first rounds against federally regulated event contracts; banks and brokers looking at prediction-market partnerships face state-by-state risk.
stories.chip: Checked on Ars Technica (opened); charge dismissal also reported by The Hill, CoinDesk and CNN; Utah filing not opened
src: Ars Technica: Kalshi makes 'difficult decision' to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
The Hill: Utah moves to dismiss criminal case against Kalshi

stories.short: Kalshi halted trading in Utah for its 177,000 users after losing court bids against the state's gambling enforcement, and a day later Utah moved to drop criminal charges against the company and its founders. The CFTC replaced 17 prediction-market waivers with one reporting rule.

stories.title: ShellBench, a benchmark built by the OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat and UC Berkeley from more than 10 million anonymised real agent interactions, finds the best models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta fail more than a third of everyday tasks, and 15.7% of attempts break at least one safety requirement (TechCrunch, 24 Nov)
stories.h: New benchmark: top AI agents fail over a third of everyday tasks
stories.ticker: ShellBench: best agents fail >1/3 of everyday tasks; 15.7% of attempts break a safety rule
stories.body:
ShellBench, built from more than 10 million anonymised real-world agent interactions by the OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat and UC Berkeley, tests the everyday errands people hand to personal agents. Even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta failed more than a third of tasks, and 15.7% of all attempts broke at least one safety requirement. It lands as Meta (Muse), OpenAI (Dots) and Anthropic (Claude Duet) push personal agents.

So what: banks deciding how far to let customers' agents act on accounts have new evidence that agents still make costly mistakes a third of the time.
stories.chip: From TechCrunch (opened); the benchmark paper was not opened
src: TechCrunch: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life

stories.title: Workday beats third-quarter forecasts (24 Nov): revenue $2.705bn, up 11.2%, adjusted EPS $2.82, subscription revenue $2.532bn, but guides fourth-quarter subscription revenue to $2.6bn, just below estimates; shares fall more than 7% after hours; it booked $51m of restructuring after cutting about 2.5% of staff
stories.h: Workday beats estimates but a soft outlook sends shares down 7% late
stories.ticker: Workday Q3 revenue $2.705bn (+11%); Q4 subscription guide light; shares -7% after hours
stories.body:
Workday reported quarterly revenue of $2.705bn (+11.2%) and adjusted EPS of $2.82, both above forecasts, with subscription revenue up 12.8% to $2.532bn and free cash flow of $691m. But its fourth-quarter subscription guide of about $2.6bn was slightly below estimates and shares fell more than 7% after hours. The quarter included $51m of restructuring after it cut about 2.5% of staff; its AI interface Sana (from a $1.1bn acquisition) is now the platform's home screen.

So what: investors are punishing software firms whose growth does not accelerate with AI; HR and finance software vendors to banks may push harder on AI add-on pricing.
stories.chip: Checked on SiliconANGLE (opened); Techmeme summary agrees; Workday release not opened

stories.title: Databricks, the data and AI platform company, is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at about a $225bn valuation, 20% above August's $190bn, the WSJ reports (24 Nov, via PYMNTS)
stories.h: Databricks seeks a $225bn valuation, the WSJ reports
stories.ticker: Databricks in early talks at ~$225bn valuation, up 20% since August (WSJ)
stories.body:
Databricks, whose platform stores company data and runs AI and analytics on it, is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at about $225bn, the Wall Street Journal reports, 20% above the $190bn it was valued at in August after a $5bn raise. The talks are early and terms could change.

So what: private AI infrastructure valuations are still rising while listed AI stocks fall; a gap that wide tends to close one way or the other.
stories.chip: WSJ report via PYMNTS (opened, partly paywalled); Databricks has not commented in what we found
src: PYMNTS: Databricks pursues $225 billion valuation months after $5 billion raise

stories.title: Marlowe, founded last year by former Microsoft Copilot Studio head Dan Lewis and AI-infrastructure lead Kutta Srinivasan, closes a $277m seed round led by Accel (24 Nov) to build inference data centres using chips from Nvidia's rivals, each tuned to one category of workload; GeekWire puts its valuation at $1.15bn
stories.h: Ex-Microsoft team raises $277m seed to build inference centres on non-Nvidia chips
stories.ticker: Marlowe: $277m seed (Accel) for workload-specific inference clusters on non-Nvidia chips
stories.body:
Marlowe raised a $277m seed round led by Accel with Bessemer, Altimeter and others; angels include the CEOs of Palo Alto Networks, Uber, Box and Dropbox. GeekWire puts its valuation at $1.15bn. Founded last year by Dan Lewis, who ran Microsoft's Copilot Studio, and Kutta Srinivasan, Marlowe builds inference data centres using chips from Nvidia's rivals, each facility tuned to one type of workload.

So what: money is flowing to the idea that inference does not need Nvidia; cheaper inference would lower the running cost of bank AI agents.
stories.chip: Checked on SiliconANGLE (opened; its body says $227m, its headline and DCD say $277m); company post not opened
src: SiliconANGLE: Marlowe raises $277M to build inference clusters with chips from Nvidia rivals

stories.title: Hong Kong gazettes legislation (reported 24 Nov) under which HKMA-supervised banks and stored-value operators would need extra registration with the SFC to offer crypto custody, trading or advice, and standalone custodians an SFC licence; the HKMA expects banks planning custody to consult it in advance and meet its safeguarding standards
stories.h: Hong Kong will make banks register with the SFC before holding clients' crypto
stories.ticker: Hong Kong bill: banks need SFC registration for crypto custody; standalone custodians need licence
stories.body:
Under a bill gazetted by the Hong Kong government, banks and stored-value facility operators supervised by the HKMA would need an additional registration with the Securities and Futures Commission to safeguard, trade, advise on or manage virtual assets for customers; independent custodians would need an SFC licence. The HKMA expects institutions planning digital-asset custody to talk to it in advance and meet its standards on segregating customer assets and safeguarding private keys. Timing depends on the legislation.

So what: banks in Hong Kong wanting to hold clients' crypto now face a dual-regulator route, which raises the bar for custody offerings.
stories.chip: From CryptoSlate (opened), which cites the government gazettal and HKMA circular; those not opened
src: CryptoSlate: Hong Kong wants banks to secure new approval before holding customers' crypto

stories.title: US prosecutors file a civil forfeiture complaint in Washington (23 Nov) to seize more than $1.1bn of USDC stolen in October's $6bn Binance hack without the attackers' keys: Circle has agreed to issue replacement USDC to the government if a court approves, while the original tokens stay frozen
stories.h: US seeks $1.1bn of stolen Binance USDC, with Circle reissuing the tokens
stories.ticker: DOJ seeks $1.1bn USDC from Binance hackers; Circle to reissue tokens if court approves
stories.body:
The Justice Department filed a civil forfeiture complaint in Washington on 23 Nov targeting more than $1.1bn of frozen USDC stolen in Binance's October hack, reported at about $6bn. Because prosecutors cannot reach the attackers' private keys, Circle has agreed to issue replacement USDC to the government if a court approves forfeiture, while the stolen tokens stay frozen. Binance is cooperating and has commissioned independent security reviews.

So what: issuer-controlled stablecoins can be frozen and reissued by court order, which matters for any bank that holds or settles in them, both as protection and as a legal exposure.
stories.chip: From CryptoSlate (opened); the DOJ complaint was not opened
src: CryptoSlate: US moves to seize $1.1 billion from Binance hackers without accessing their wallets

stories.title: Colorado says (24 Nov) a cyberattack discovered on 18 Nov took down the myColorado app, used by 2.1 million residents for digital ID, documents and state services, and likely stole data tied to nearly 150,000 people; the app is still offline
stories.h: Cyberattack takes down Colorado's digital ID app and steals data on 150,000
stories.ticker: myColorado digital ID app offline after breach; data of ~150,000 likely stolen
stories.body:
Colorado's Office of Information Technology says hackers breached the myColorado app, which 2.1 million residents use for digital ID, document storage and state services, on the evening of 18 Nov. The app remains offline, and data tied to nearly 150,000 people was likely stolen; the state has not said what data.

So what: state digital IDs are becoming identity-verification inputs for bank onboarding; a breach of one is a fraud risk for KYC teams.
stories.chip: From The Record (opened), quoting the state's statement
src: The Record: Colorado says cyberattack took down myColorado app, warns 150,000 had data stolen

stories.title: Anthropic publishes 'Working with AI' (23 Nov), interviews with people at 58 companies that use Claude: they describe few layoffs but reduced hiring, and say the most valuable uses involved reorganising roles and workplaces around AI
stories.h: Anthropic study: AI brings fewer hires rather than layoffs at 58 companies
stories.ticker: Anthropic interviews 58 Claude-using firms: few layoffs, reduced hiring
stories.body:
Anthropic's economics team interviewed people at 58 companies that use Claude. They described few layoffs but reduced hiring, and said the most valuable uses of AI often came from reorganising roles and workplaces around it rather than bolting it onto existing jobs. The study comes from the company selling the tool and covers only its customers.

So what: the first labour effect is on entry-level hiring, not on existing staff; graduate and analyst intakes are where banks will see it first.
stories.chip: Summary checked on Anthropic's research index (opened); full report not read

stories.title: Uber and Nuro begin testing Lucid Gravity robotaxis with no safety driver on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area (from 23 Nov) ahead of a planned 2027 commercial launch
stories.h: Uber and Nuro start driverless tests of Lucid robotaxis in the Bay Area
stories.ticker: Uber/Nuro pull safety drivers from Lucid Gravity robotaxis in Bay Area tests; 2027 launch
stories.body:
Uber and Nuro have started testing Lucid Gravity SUVs with no one in the driver's seat on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area, ahead of a commercial robotaxi launch planned for 2027. It comes as Waymo, the market leader there, recalls vehicles over closed freeway lanes and paused service for storms.

So what: a second large robotaxi fleet is nearing the Bay Area; motor insurers and auto lenders should expect liability to keep shifting from drivers to operators.

stories.title: Quad9, the non-profit public DNS resolver, switches off service for all users in France (24 Nov, 09:00 Paris time) rather than comply with court-upheld demands from sports rightsholder beIN to block piracy streaming domains, after facing fines
stories.h: Quad9 switches off its DNS service in France rather than block piracy sites
stories.ticker: Quad9 disables DNS service in France over beIN piracy-blocking orders
stories.body:
Quad9, a non-profit public DNS resolver (9.9.9.9), disabled its service for all users in France on 24 Nov rather than obey court-backed demands from sports broadcaster beIN to block domains linked to piracy streams. It had been fined for not complying. Quad9 says it opposes piracy but that forcing resolvers to block content does nothing to the servers that host it. The story drew 342 points on Hacker News.

So what: anyone in France using 9.9.9.9 for filtering malicious domains, including some corporate networks, needs a new resolver.
stories.chip: Checked on Quad9's own notice (opened)

stories.title: The Court of Arbitration for Sport reinstates Senegal as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions (24 Nov), overturning a decision that stripped them of the title after they walked off in protest at a stoppage-time penalty in January's final against hosts Morocco; Morocco vows further legal action
stories.h: Court reinstates Senegal as Africa Cup of Nations champions, ten months on
stories.ticker: CAS reinstates Senegal as AFCON 2025 winners; Morocco vows further action
stories.body:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled that Senegal are the winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations, overturning the decision that stripped them of the title they won on the pitch in January. With the final against hosts Morocco goalless in stoppage time, Senegal had left the field in protest at a penalty awarded against them, delaying the match in Rabat by more than 15 minutes. Morocco says it will take further legal action.

So what: ten months after the final, the title is still in court, which shows how far sports governance disputes now run through lawyers.
stories.chip: Checked on BBC Sport (opened); also France 24, Africanews and The Independent
src: BBC Sport: Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling
The Independent: Morocco vow further legal action after Senegal reinstated

stories.update: Pressure moves to Washington: Trump says a pardon for Huang is 'an option' he doesn't expect to need, the attorney general won't say whether DOJ or the FBI investigated him, Megaspeed is now on the Entity List, and Nvidia shares give back 5.9%.
stories.title: A day after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang, President Trump tells the New York Post (24 Nov) that pardoning him is 'an option' but probably not necessary; Attorney General Todd Blanche calls Nvidia a 'good corporate citizen' but repeatedly declines to say whether the DOJ or FBI has investigated Huang; Commerce adds Megaspeed and subsidiaries to the Entity List, which trade experts say omits a usual clause; lawmakers from both parties criticise the reinstatement; Huang faces questions from House committees on 1 Dec; Nvidia falls 5.9% to $155.38
stories.h: Trump calls a Huang pardon 'an option' as Congress prepares its questions
stories.ticker: Trump: Huang pardon 'an option'; AG won't say if DOJ probed him; NVDA -5.9% to $155.38
stories.body:
President Trump told the New York Post that pardoning Jensen Huang is "always an option" but he doesn't think it will be necessary. Attorney General Todd Blanche called Nvidia a "good corporate citizen" but, asked repeatedly whether the DOJ or FBI had investigated Huang, said: "I don't know what you're talking about." The Commerce Department has now added Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud firm linked to Alice Huang, and its subsidiaries to the Entity List; trade experts say the rule leaves out a clause such listings usually include. Hakeem Jeffries called the reinstatement "indefensible"; Republican Don Bacon called it "inexplicable". Huang is due to face House committees in a recorded interview on 1 Dec and the Senate Banking Committee later. Nvidia fell 5.9% to $155.38.

So what: talk of a pardon before any charge keeps the legal and governance risk around Nvidia open; banks with Nvidia exposure should watch the 1 Dec interview and any DOJ statement.
stories.chip: Checked on TechCrunch, BBC and SiliconANGLE (all opened); NY Post interview not opened
src: TechCrunch: Trump reportedly says pardoning Jensen Huang is 'an option'
BBC: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
SiliconANGLE: Congress scrutinizes Jensen Huang's return as Megaspeed restrictions raise questions
stories.short: Trump says pardoning Jensen Huang is 'an option' he doesn't expect to need, and the attorney general won't say whether the DOJ or FBI investigated him. Megaspeed is now on the Entity List. Huang faces House committees on 1 Dec, and Nvidia shares fell 5.9% on Tuesday.
